synthesis.headline: Deep central trough brings Texas flooding and Ohio Valley storms; Trudy to become major hurricane off Mexico
synthesis.narrative:
A deep, still-open trough over the central US is pushing a strong cold front east. Behind it, a 1040 mb high drives a sharp cooldown, from 10-15 F above normal in the East today to 15-20 below across the central US Friday. Yesterday's southern Plains flood threat has narrowed to Texas, where WPC has a Moderate excessive-rainfall risk near the Rio Grande (the exact placement is uncertain) inside a Slight risk across central Texas. SPC has a Marginal severe risk from southern Illinois to southern Ohio, for damaging gusts and a brief tornado or two. Offshore, Hurricane Trudy (75 mph, 989 mb, about 300 miles SSW of Acapulco) is forecast to intensify rapidly to a major hurricane Friday, peaking near 130 mph Saturday. It is expected to pass very close to the coast from Punta San Telmo to Cabo Corrientes. Colima and Jalisco face 4-8 inches of rain, isolated 12, with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

At 500 mb, closed highs near the Pacific Northwest coast (588 dam) and the Carolina coast (594 dam) bracket the trough, whose base sits near 576-580 dam over Texas. Flow of 90-100 kt at 500 mb gives strong shear on its eastern flank. But the Atlantic ridge slows the trough, and the Texas front is turning anafrontal, so the threat there is repeated heavy rain, not severe storms. Trudy turns west away from the coast early next week as shear and dry air weaken it; the day 4-5 track is uncertain. Tropical Storm Simon (60 mph), stalled south-southeast of Cabo San Lucas, should pass near or west of Baja California Sur this weekend and weaken.

On Friday, SPC has a Slight severe risk for the Mid-Atlantic, mainly damaging gusts, with a brief tornado possible near Delmarva. No flash-flood risk is drawn for Friday. Frost and freeze are possible in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast Sunday and Monday. Models now hint at a low lingering off the Mid-Atlantic coast next week, but they disagree on how close. In the West, an upper low brings rain and high-elevation snow Tuesday and Wednesday. The eastern cooldown interrupts the warm eastern pattern rather than ending it: 6-10 day heights turn above normal again over the central and eastern US, with a negative anomaly near the Four Corners. The 8-14 day chart instead pulls the ridge back toward the Southwest and northern Mexico, so week two is unsettled.
synthesis.climate_context: A very strong El Niño frames the tropics. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 C for July-September, up 0.3 to 0.5 C each season since spring, with no sign of peaking. That fits a still-busy East Pacific hurricane season deep into October: two storms are active, Trudy is set to become a major hurricane, and another system may form next week. It also fits a quiet Atlantic: NHC expects no development there for seven days, as El Niño-driven shear typically suppresses the basin. Over the continent, mid-October's strong jet and returning Gulf moisture support the autumn severe and heavy-rain flare-up seen this week.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has issued no mesoscale discussions in the last six hours. Texas storms behind the front pose only an isolated wet-microburst risk (a water-loaded gust); the threat there is flooding. NHC says watches are likely for southwestern Mexico, with tropical-storm-force winds possible by Saturday and dangerous surf from Friday. Outer bands could drop 2-4 inches, locally 6, from Guerrero to Michoacan, and Simon brings 1-2 inches, locally 3, to Baja California Sur. NHC gives a new low off southern Mexico a 30% chance of forming next week.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 12Z Thursday October 15 analysis is dominated by a cold front sweeping the northern and central US. A low near the Minnesota/Ontario border (about 1014 mb) anchors a long cold front trailing south and west through the Dakotas and into the central Rockies, with a second low near the Kansas/Missouri area (about 1014 mb) along the same boundary. Another low of roughly 1013 mb sits over the southern Plains in northwest Texas and Oklahoma, and a weak low of about 1015 mb is analyzed over the Southwest. The strongest pressure feature is a large high over the northern Rockies and northern Plains, with closed isobars near 1040 mb, a genuinely strong cool-season ridge that is the source of the cooler air behind the front. A separate high of about 1029 mb sits over Ontario and the Great Lakes, and a 1021 mb high over the Southeast and Carolinas is modest and mostly guides flow rather than driving weather.

The pressure gradient is tightest on the northwest flank of the low near Minnesota and along the northern Plains between the 1040 mb high and the front, where isobars are packed and winds are plotted strong from the north and northwest. Gradient is slack across the Southeast, the central Appalachians, and the lower Mississippi Valley, with only light winds around the 1021 mb high.

A second boundary, drawn as a stationary or warm front, stretches along the mid-Atlantic coast from Virginia and the Carolinas toward the Atlantic, with a short segment of cold front in the Florida Panhandle and Gulf area. Lift and moisture focus along the Plains cold front from the Minnesota low into Kansas and Oklahoma, where dewpoints in the 60s and low 70s F sit ahead of the front, and along the southern Plains low where Gulf moisture streams north. The mid-Atlantic coastal boundary is a second convergence zone with warm, humid air to its south.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This is the CMC surface analysis valid 00Z Thursday 15 October 2026, on a polar projection, so the upper half of the frame is Arctic ocean and archipelago rather than southern Canada. The deepest centers sit in the far north: a 944 mb low in the upper right and a 971 mb low just left of it, both well into the high Arctic, with a 982-985 mb pair of lows to their left. A 969 mb low with a wide field of closely packed isobars occupies the upper left, near the edge of the domain and well away from the provinces. These are strong cyclones, but their position over the polar basin and archipelago puts them in the range of ordinary autumn Arctic activity, and the tight gradients around them stay north of the Canadian mainland.

Over the continent itself the pattern is much weaker. Highs of 1024 to 1030 mb are scattered across the central and western interior of North America, with a 1030 mb center and another 1027 mb center near the middle of the continent, suggesting a broad, flat ridge across the Prairies and northern Plains. A 1017 mb low sits north of these highs and a 1011 mb low lies along the cold front trailing south and west from the Great Lakes region, though the chart is crowded enough that I would not pin either low to a specific province.

The most organized cross-border feature is the long cold front running from the Great Lakes area southwest into the central United States, with a weak 1006 mb low on a trailing boundary over the south-central states and further lows of 1013 to 1015 mb along the front. Isobar spacing along this boundary is wide, so the gradient and likely wind are modest, but the front is the clearest focus for lift and moisture linking Canadian airmass contrast to the U.S. interior. A second, shorter front with a 1000 mb low lies over the northeastern part of the continent near the Atlantic edge, and a frontal wave appears off the east coast.

On the Pacific side, a 997 mb low with an occluded system sits at the far left of the frame, with a long trailing cold front arcing southwest across the northern Pacific toward the western edge of the chart. Another large low of roughly 987 mb near the Gulf of Alaska region feeds a cold front sweeping south along the western coast, the main moisture focus for the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia coast, though the exact coastal placement is hard to confirm at this scale.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 500 mb analysis for 1200 UTC 15 Oct 2026 shows a high-amplitude pattern: ridging over the Pacific Northwest and western Canada (a closed high near the coast, contours near 588 dam) and a strong, broad ridge over the southeastern US and western Atlantic (closed high near the Carolina coast, 594 dam contours). Between them sits a deep longwave trough over the central US, with the base near the southern Plains (Texas/Oklahoma area, heights roughly 576-580 dam) and the axis extending northward into the northern Plains and Canadian Prairies, where the 5400-5600 m contours (540-560 dam) show cold air aloft. This is an amplified ridge-trough-ridge configuration, not a Rex block, since no closed low sits beneath a poleward anticyclone.

The trough is not obviously closed off: the height contours over the Plains remain open and wrap through the base, so it still appears connected to the westerlies. Its orientation looks positively tilted to neutral, with the southern base pushing east-northeastward toward the lower Mississippi Valley, and the implied downstream flow is southwesterly. A compact wind maximum is visible in the shaded speeds (olive/brown, roughly 45-55 kt) across the northern Plains into the Upper Midwest, and a second isolated maximum appears over north Texas/Oklahoma, consistent with a shortwave rotating through the trough base.

The strongest winds on the chart are in the far northeast, where the shading reaches red (95+ kt) over New England and the adjacent Atlantic: a powerful jet streak on the downstream side of the central trough, curving around the northwest flank of the western Atlantic ridge. The tight packing of contours there marks a strong height gradient along the implied jet corridor.

Overall the flow is amplified and slow-moving rather than zonal, though it is not a true block. With the Pacific ridge upstream and the Atlantic ridge downstream, the central US trough is bracketed and likely to progress only slowly eastward.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The dominant feature is a long, southwest-to-northeast oriented cloud band running from the Texas Hill Country and the Rio Grande region of southwest Texas up through Oklahoma, Kansas, Iowa and Minnesota toward the upper Great Lakes. This cloud shield, white to tan in the composite, marks the frontal zone and is accompanied along its western flank by a dry streamer. Orange-red dry air extends from the northern Rockies and High Plains of Montana, Wyoming and Colorado southeastward behind the cloud band, with the most saturated orange along the Dakotas and Nebraska. The sharp contrast between this dry air and the moist green and olive air ahead of it over the Mississippi Valley and Southeast is the likely jet corridor, implied rather than measured.

Farther west, a darker blue-purple area along the Pacific Northwest coast and offshore, with bright white cloud near the limb, points to a cold, dry upper troposphere with an approaching system. The compact, elongated dry features wrapping the cyclonic side of the flow over the northern Plains are the best candidates for stratospheric-intrusion character, though descent itself cannot be confirmed from this imagery.

East of the front, the Southeast, Gulf Coast and western Atlantic are covered in broad green to olive-brown tones, consistent with moist tropical air and little organized cloud. A deeper orange-red patch over the Gulf of Mexico southwest of Florida and near the Texas coast looks like dry air aloft, probably tied to upper-level flow rather than a compact intrusion. A separate orange-red area in the far northeast, over Quebec and the Canadian Maritimes, is another dry feature on the cyclonic side of the flow there.

Organized deep convection is limited to scattered bright cloud clusters over the northwest Caribbean, near Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, and off the Pacific coast of southern Mexico and Central America, with none clearly linked to a closed circulation in this view.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 13:20Z on 15 October shows the most organized convection in the eastern Pacific, where a compact comma-shaped cloud mass with a curved band sits well south of Mexico near 100W. This is consistent with a developing tropical cyclone, though the image alone cannot confirm its intensity. Scattered bright convective clusters extend westward and southeastward along the Pacific ITCZ toward Central America and Colombia, with additional white cloud over the western Caribbean and the northern Andes.

In the Atlantic, a rounded spiral of green and orange moisture at roughly 20N, 45W in the central basin appears to be a mid-level or upper cyclonic circulation with little deep cloud, so it looks non-tropical or at least non-convective at this time. Farther northeast, a compact cloud swirl near 25N, 28W is a separate small cyclonic feature, with broad white cloud at higher latitudes to its north and east.

Across Canada and the Arctic, the northern edge of the disk is dominated by purple and blue shades, indicating cold, dry upper-tropospheric air on the poleward side of the flow. The sharpest change to green and orange tones across southern Canada and the northern tier of the United States marks the airmass boundary, with the implied polar jet corridor running along it from the northern Rockies toward the Great Lakes and Labrador. A bright cloud shield over Labrador and the Canadian Maritimes, bordered by red-orange dry air, suggests a mature system there. Viewing-angle distortion near the limb makes high-latitude positions approximate.

In the Southern Hemisphere, the swirls of saturated red-orange off southern Chile and near Patagonia mark compact dry intrusions wrapped into cyclonic circulations. Those are the features here that best fit high-PV, stratospheric-origin air. Tropical South America is largely green and moist, with a large convective complex over eastern Brazil.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This CPC outlook for October 20-24, 2026 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the central and eastern U.S., with probabilities that climb eastward from the Rockies. The strongest signal sits over the Upper Mississippi Valley and western Great Lakes, where a 70-80% category (the darkest shading on the map) covers Iowa, Missouri, much of Illinois and Wisconsin, and the Minnesota border region. Surrounding that core, a broad 60-70% area spans the Plains, Mid-South, Texas and Ohio Valley, with 50-60% over the southern Plains, Gulf coast, Southeast and mid-Atlantic, tapering to 33-50% along the Northeast and Atlantic coasts, the northern Rockies and High Plains.

The only cool signal is in the West. A below-normal area of 33-40% covers California, western Nevada and the Pacific Northwest interior, with a small 40-50% pocket over central California and western Nevada. It is bordered by a near-normal (equal chances) zone through the Intermountain West, and Maine's northeastern tip and much of mainland Alaska are also near normal. Hawaii and the southern Alaska coast lean above.

These are probabilities of tercile category, not temperature departures, so the chart does not give magnitudes. The pattern is consistent with a western trough or cooler flow and a downstream ridge over the central and eastern U.S., with the warmth peaking under the implied ridge axis near the Mississippi Valley. That reading is inferred, since no height field is plotted. The tight west-to-east gradient from below to above normal suggests the outlook expects this configuration to hold through the 6-10 day period rather than break down. The sharp gradient across the Rockies also indicates the tools agree on a fairly stable pattern, though the near-normal and low-probability zones in the interior West mark where timing of any trough progression is least certain.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly prognostic, made 14 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 20-24. Solid green contours are heights, labeled in meters (5100 to 5820 m, i.e. 510 to 582 dam, so a 582 dam contour crosses the southern Plains); the dashed lines are anomalies, with red positive, blue negative and purple the zero line, labeled at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. Note the labels read as multiples of 30 (-30, 0, 30), so the plotted units appear to be meters, not dam, and the anomaly contour spacing is uncertain from the text alone.

The dominant feature is a deep Arctic low near 80-85N, roughly north of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Alaska side of the pole, with a closed center near 5100 m and negative anomalies of about -90 m in its core. Heights rise steeply southward, with a tightly packed band of contours across Canada, so the implied westerly flow is strong and fairly zonal north of about 50N.

Positive anomalies are broad and weak-to-moderate. A positive area covers the central and eastern US and southeast Canada (30 m labels over the Midwest and near the Mid-Atlantic coast), with another positive region over the southern Plains and Texas. Over the Greenland and North Atlantic sector, large positive values appear near the top right (labels of 150 and 210 in the red dashed field), which look implausibly large for an anomaly; the plotted units or label reading there are doubtful, and I would treat them as likely a misread or a high-latitude artifact rather than true departures.

Over the western US the picture is the opposite of a persistent western ridge: a negative anomaly centered near the Four Corners and Great Basin region (about -30 m), with the zero line wrapping around it from the Pacific Northwest coast to northern Mexico. The ridge axis is displaced east of the Rockies, running roughly from the southern Plains north through the Great Lakes, while a trough axis sits over the Intermountain West and Southwest, with a second weaker trough implied offshore in the Pacific.

The sense of this pattern is a retreat of western ridging eastward, with the zero-anomaly line reaching deep into the interior West, and a flatter, more zonal flow across southern Canada.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic, made 14 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 22-28. The solid green contours are heights (labeled in meters, 5160 to 5880 m, i.e. 516-588 dam) and the dashed lines are anomalies at 60 m (6 dam) intervals; the sign of the dashed contours is hard to read at this resolution, so the following is based on the plotted geometry and labels. The dominant feature is a deep trough with a closed low near 516 dam centered over the Arctic Ocean/Canadian Arctic, with tightly packed contours encircling the pole and a strong height gradient running from the Pacific Northwest across southern Canada to the Great Lakes and Northeast. A blue dashed closed contour near the pole and another over the Labrador/Davis Strait region indicate negative anomalies there, with the Arctic one labeled around -60 m (about -6 dam).

Over western Canada, the northern Rockies and northern Plains I do not see a closed positive anomaly center; the contours there run west to east and sag southward toward the Great Lakes (5640 to 5700 m near the US-Canada border), which implies zonal to cyclonic flow rather than a ridge. A red dashed anomaly line encloses much of the Rockies and Plains, but it is not clearly a closed positive core, so any height rise there looks weak at best, and the labels I can read near it (a 30 and a 130) are not legible enough to quantify.

The ridge axis appears displaced well south and west: the 5820 and 5880 m contours bow northward over the Southwest and northern Mexico, with higher heights offshore in the eastern Pacific off Baja and along the Gulf of Mexico. In other words the ridge looks to have retreated to the Southwest and northern Mexico rather than remaining over the northern Rockies. This is a read of the contour geometry; the exact anomaly magnitude of that ridge is uncertain from this image.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary:
This Day 1 outlook, valid 12Z Thursday October 15 through 12Z Friday October 16, 2026, shows three categories: Marginal, Slight and Moderate. No High risk is drawn. The highest category, Moderate (at least 40% chance of exceeding flash-flood guidance within 25 miles of a point), is a small red area over south Texas, in the southern part of the state near the Rio Grande and the lower Texas coastal plain; the border and coastline in that corner are only roughly resolved, so the exact placement is approximate. A Slight risk (yellow) wraps around the Moderate area and extends northeast across central Texas toward the Texas-Oklahoma border area.

The broad Marginal risk (green) forms a long, narrow southwest-to-northeast band. It runs from south Texas across eastern Texas and the Red River vicinity, then through Arkansas and the Mississippi Valley region into the Ohio Valley, ending near Kentucky or southern Ohio. A separate small Marginal area sits over western Virginia or the central Appalachians, apart from the main band.

The elongated, linear shape of the risk axis is what you would expect along a slow-moving or stalled frontal boundary, with the most concentrated risk where repeated heavy rain is most likely in south and central Texas. The chart itself does not show a front, a tropical system or terrain forcing, so that is an inference from the geometry; nothing visible points to a tropical origin, and the Appalachian Marginal area may reflect terrain influence. The chart gives risk categories only, not rainfall amounts.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Friday October 16 through 12Z Saturday October 17, 2026, has no risk areas drawn anywhere on the map. A text box across the central United States states that the probability of rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance is less than 5 percent, which is below the threshold for even the Marginal category, the lowest of the four (Marginal, Slight, Moderate, High). No green, orange, red or magenta contours appear over the contiguous states, so none of the four categories are in play from the West Coast to the Atlantic seaboard or along the Gulf Coast. Day 1 is not shown here, so I cannot say whether any earlier risk has relaxed or shifted; all that is evident is that the flash-flood threat is minimal for this period. Note that this speaks only to flash-flood-scale excessive rainfall, so ordinary showers or lighter, beneficial rain could still occur in places without approaching flood guidance.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 208 AM EDT Thursday, October 15, 2026 (valid through 12Z Saturday, October 17), an unsettled pattern covers the central and eastern U.S. A frontal boundary stretches from the Mid-Atlantic through the Ohio Valley to the Plains, with a surface low over the southern High Plains moving northeast toward the Great Lakes. Gulf moisture will fuel repeated rounds of showers and storms.

Thursday brings flash flood risk. A Moderate Risk of excessive rainfall covers west Texas, a Slight Risk covers a wider area of Texas, and a Marginal Risk covers the Midwest, Ohio Valley, and Mid-Atlantic. Isolated severe storms capable of damaging winds, hail, and a brief tornado are possible from the Mid-Mississippi Valley through the Ohio Valley/Great Lakes and Texas.

Friday, the Storm Prediction Center has a severe risk for the Mid-Atlantic as instability and shear increase. The cold front then reaches the Atlantic Coast and southern states, with lingering storms over Florida and the Mid-Atlantic/Northeast. Showers persist in the Pacific Northwest.

Temperatures swing from 10 to 15 degrees above normal in the East Thursday to 15 to 20 degrees below normal across the central U.S. and spreading east Friday, with highs mostly in the 50s and 60s.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Issued 0752 AM CDT Thursday, October 15, 2026, valid 1300Z October 15 to 1200Z October 16. A marginal risk of severe thunderstorms covers portions of the mid Mississippi and Ohio Valleys. Storms may produce isolated severe wind gusts and perhaps a tornado or two. A deep upper trough moving from the Canadian Prairies toward the Upper Midwest will bring 90 to 100 kt of 500 mb flow to its eastern periphery from central Illinois across Lower Michigan. A surface low over southeast Kansas will deepen as it moves northeast. Upper 60s to low 70s dewpoints will spread north across the lower and upper Ohio Valley, supporting modest buoyancy. The best combination of shear and buoyancy is expected near or just south of the warm front, from southern Illinois through southern Ohio. Bowing segments could produce damaging gusts, and curved low-level hodographs support a few brief tornadoes. Severe probabilities were not introduced near the low over northern Illinois. In west and central Texas, showers and storms ahead of a slow-moving cold front will take on a more anafrontal character, with severe potential limited to an isolated water-loaded gust.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours, so no organized convective threat is currently being actively monitored by the Storm Prediction Center. This reflects only that six-hour window. It does not rule out convection developing later, and it says nothing about the outlook for the coming hours or days, which is covered by other SPC products.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic (as of 800 AM EDT Thu Oct 15 2026): The National Hurricane Center expects no tropical cyclone formation in the North Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, or Gulf of America during the next 7 days.

East Pacific (as of 500 AM PDT Thu Oct 15 2026): Two active systems are being advised on. Tropical Storm Simon is a few hundred miles south-southeast of the southern tip of the Baja California Peninsula. Hurricane Trudy, recently upgraded, is several hundred miles south-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico.

A separate area of low pressure is expected to form offshore of southern Mexico in the early to middle part of next week. Conditions appear conducive to gradual development afterward as it moves generally west to west-northwest over the eastern and central East Pacific. Formation chance through 48 hours is near 0 percent. Formation chance through 7 days is 30 percent.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
As of 2026-10-15 09:00 UTC, NHC is tracking two Eastern Pacific systems.

Hurricane Trudy, a Category 1 hurricane, is centered near 12.9N 101.6W, about 300 miles SSW of Acapulco. Maximum sustained winds are 75 mph (65 kt) and the minimum pressure is 989 mb. It is moving NW at 9 mph. Rapid intensification is forecast over the next 24 hours, with Trudy becoming a major hurricane by Friday and peaking near 130 mph around Saturday. Shear and dry air should cause weakening by day 3. Trudy is forecast to pass very close to the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico, from near Punta San Telmo to Cabo Corrientes, this weekend, then turn west away from the coast early next week. Track uncertainty is considerable for days 4 and 5. Tropical-storm-force winds could reach the coast as early as Saturday. No coastal watches or warnings are in effect, but watches are likely later this morning. Hurricane-force winds extend 25 miles from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend 115 miles. Rainfall of 4 to 8 inches, with isolated totals near 12 inches, is expected through the weekend in Colima and Jalisco, posing life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Outer bands could bring 2 to 4 inches, locally 6, to the coast from Guerrero to Michoacan. Swells from Trudy will reach southwestern Mexico from Friday and could cause life-threatening surf and rip currents.

Tropical Storm Simon is centered near 19.2N 108.5W, about 270 miles SSE of Cabo San Lucas. Maximum sustained winds are 60 mph (50 kt) and the minimum pressure is 996 mb. It is nearly stationary and expected to meander before turning northwest on Friday. Simon should pass near or west of Baja California Sur this weekend and weaken, likely becoming post-tropical by about 72 hours, possibly sooner. The storm is small, with tropical-storm-force winds extending 35 miles. No watches or warnings are in effect. Rainfall of 1 to 2 inches, locally 3, is expected in Baja California Sur through early Saturday. Swells will affect west-central Mexico and Baja California Sur, with life-threatening surf and rip currents likely.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ENSO state per the Oceanic Niño Index: El Niño conditions are present and strengthening quickly. The three-month running mean anomaly rose each season from -0.39 C in DJF 2026, through near-neutral values in FMA (+0.11 C) and MAM (+0.46 C), and crossed the +0.5 C El Niño threshold in AMJ 2026 (+0.95 C). It then reached +1.39 C in MJJ, +1.80 C in JJA, and +2.16 C in JAS 2026, the most recent season listed. The JAS value is in the very strong El Niño range (at or above +2.0 C). The associated total SST value is 29.12 C for JAS. Since spring, the anomaly has risen by roughly 0.3 to 0.5 C per season. The table carries no issue date, so confirm the latest season against the current CPC release.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Observed CPC teleconnection indices as of 2026-09-30, flagged STALE: the newest value for all three indices is 15 days old and has not been updated, so do not treat these as current.

PNA: latest +0.12. The 7-day mean is -0.41, up 1.10 from the prior week's -1.51. Daily values were negative for most of the window and turned positive only in the last two days, which would favor western North American ridging with eastern troughing if sustained.

AO: latest -0.26. The 7-day mean is +0.04, down 1.69 from +1.73 the prior week. Values have fallen from strongly positive to near zero and now slightly negative, a drift that would favor high-latitude blocking if it continues.

NAO: latest -0.78. The 7-day mean is -0.15, down 0.43 from +0.28. This is the most negative reading in the window and is falling, which bears on whether an eastern cutoff can escape.

Summer teleconnections are weaker and less canonical than in winter. Treat these as directional support only, not as evidence on their own.
